--- title: "Wedge-tailed eagle energy harvesting" subtitle: "Fitting behavioural bouts to landscape features - XGBoost" author: - name: "Scott Forrest" url: https://swforrest.github.io/ orcid: 0000-0001-9529-0108 affiliation: University of Tasmania, QUT email: "scottwforrest@gmail.com" - name: "James Pay" affiliation: University of Tasmania date: "2026-11-25" execute: cache: false warning: false bibliography: references.bib toc: true number-sections: false format: html: # self-contained: true code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" code-tools: true df-print: paged code-line-numbers: true code-overflow: scroll fig-format: png fig-dpi: 150 editor: source editor_options: chunk_output_type: inline abstract: | Here we use the behavioural states estimated by the classification methods to identify where and when wedge-tailed eagles 'harvest' environmental energy by soaring. As an alternative to the random forest (`energy_harvesting_random_forest.qmd`), we relate the soaring bouts (with flapping bouts as the negative samples) to the time of day, the day of the year and static landscape features such as topography, using gradient boosted trees (XGBoost). We use the same data, predictors and cross-validation folds as the random forest, so the two methods can be compared directly. The number of boosting rounds and the tree settings are chosen by day-blocked cross-validation with early stopping, and the model is interpreted with permutation importance, accumulated local effects and SHAP values (including SHAP interaction values, to look for interactions between the time and the landscape). We then map the relative suitability for soaring at different times of the day and year. --- # Load packages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) packages <- c("terra", "tidyterra", "sf", "xgboost", # gradient boosted trees "blockCV", # spatial blocks for cross-validation "pROC", # AUC and thresholds "iml", # accumulated local effects "suncalc") # sunrise and sunset walk(packages, require, character.only = T) ``` ::: # Settings All of the settings that might need changing are in this one chunk. - `eagle_name` - the eagle to model. This reads that eagle's bouts from `energy_harvesting_data_prep.qmd` (run that script for the same eagle first), and the outputs are saved in a separate folder for each eagle. Run the random forest script for the same eagle first, so the two methods are compared for the same eagle - `seed` - the random seed. It is the same as in the random forest script, so that the random and day-blocked folds are the same - `learning_rate`, `max_rounds` and `early_stopping_rounds` - how the number of boosting rounds is chosen (see the tuning section) - `n_threads` - the number of CPU threads that XGBoost uses - the number of folds for each type of cross-validation, and the size of the spatial blocks (the same as in the random forest script, where these were chosen) - `test_run` - set to `TRUE` to run everything on a random 20% of the days, which is quicker when testing changes to the script - `out_dir` - the folder for the model, predictions, tables and rasters made by this script, and `rf_dir` - the folder with the random forest outputs (for the comparison between the methods) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the eagle to model eagle_name <- "Tabatha" # random seed for the folds, permutations and models (the same as the random forest) seed <- 2026 # local time zone (for the date and day of year) local_tz <- "Australia/Hobart" # XGBoost settings learning_rate <- 0.05 # how much each new tree changes the predictions (eta) max_rounds <- 3000 # the most boosting rounds (trees) to try early_stopping_rounds <- 50 # stop when the held-out log loss hasn't improved in this many rounds n_threads <- 4 # number of CPU threads # number of folds for each cross-validation scheme n_folds_random <- 10 n_folds_day <- 10 n_folds_spatial <- 5 # width of the square spatial blocks (m) block_size_m <- 2000 # number of times each variable is shuffled for the permutation importance n_permutations <- 5 # TRUE to only use a random 20% of the days (for testing changes to the script) test_run <- FALSE # folder for the outputs of this script, and the folder with the random forest # outputs (one for each eagle) out_dir <- paste0("outputs/xgboost_", eagle_name) rf_dir <- paste0("outputs/random_forest_", eagle_name) dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE) # colours for each behaviour (the same as in the other scripts) behaviour_colours <- c(soaring = "#E69F00", flapping = "#56B4E9") ``` ::: # Import data from `energy_harvesting_data_prep.qmd` The data preparation in this section is the same as in the random forest script - see that script for the map of the bouts, and the plots of the predictors and the correlations between them. Each row is a soaring or flapping bout (at least 30 seconds of that behaviour, with a new bout starting after a gap of more than 60 seconds), with the values of the landscape variables at the start location of the bout. `soaring` is the response: 1 for a soaring bout and 0 for a flapping bout. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} combined_bouts <- read_csv(paste0("outputs/combined_bouts_consensus_", eagle_name, ".csv")) # number of bouts of each behaviour for each eagle combined_bouts %>% count(name, behaviour) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Time variables We describe when each bout happened with two variables, both calculated at the start of the bout (the same point in time and place as the landscape variables). **Day fraction** (`day_fraction`) - the time of day relative to sunrise and sunset: 0 is sunrise, 1 is sunset and 0.5 is (very close to) solar noon. Times before sunrise are negative and times after sunset are above 1. Scaling the time to the daylight period makes the same value comparable through the year (whereas 9 am is about 3 hours after sunrise in mid-summer, but only 1.5 hours in mid-winter). The sunrise and sunset times are calculated with `suncalc` for the local date and the start location of each bout. **Day of the year** (`yday`) is circular, so we split it into its sine and cosine. `yday_cos` is roughly a summer (1) to winter (-1) axis, and `yday_sin` separates autumn (1) from spring (-1). When interpreting the model we treat them as one variable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} combined_bouts <- combined_bouts %>% mutate( # local date and day of the year date_local = as_date(with_tz(start, local_tz)), yday = yday(date_local), # day of the year around a circle yday_sin = sin(2 * pi * yday / 365.25), yday_cos = cos(2 * pi * yday / 365.25) ) # sunrise and sunset on the local date at the start location of each bout # (getSunlightTimes returns one row for each row of data, in the same order) bout_sun_times <- getSunlightTimes(data = data.frame(date = combined_bouts$date_local, lat = combined_bouts$lat, lon = combined_bouts$lon), keep = c("sunrise", "sunset"), tz = "UTC") # check that the rows are in the same order (should be TRUE) all(bout_sun_times$date == combined_bouts$date_local & bout_sun_times$lat == combined_bouts$lat) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} combined_bouts <- combined_bouts %>% mutate(sunrise = bout_sun_times$sunrise, sunset = bout_sun_times$sunset, # time since sunrise as a fraction of the time from sunrise to sunset # (0 = sunrise, 1 = sunset, negative before sunrise, above 1 after sunset) day_fraction = as.numeric(difftime(start, sunrise, units = "secs")) / as.numeric(difftime(sunset, sunrise, units = "secs"))) # the range of day fractions summary(combined_bouts$day_fraction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. -0.0437 0.4081 0.5381 0.5367 0.6623 1.0520 ``` ::: ::: ## Predictor variables The predictors are the same as for the random forest - the time variables and the topographic variables at the start location of each bout. As for the random forest, we never use variables that describe the movement itself (bout duration, altitude gained, vertical rate, flight height), the eagle's name, the coordinates or the clock time (see the random forest script for why). We also define the same groups of related predictors as for the random forest, which are used for the grouped importance (slope and ruggedness are highly correlated, and the sine and cosine of the day of year only make sense together). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the variables used in the models, in groups time_vars <- c("day_fraction", "yday_sin", "yday_cos") landscape_vars <- c("elevation", "tpi_300m", "slope", "ruggedness", "northness", "eastness") predictors <- c(time_vars, landscape_vars) # labels for the plots variable_labels <- c(day_fraction = "Day fraction (0 = sunrise, 1 = sunset)", yday_sin = "Day of year (sine)", yday_cos = "Day of year (cosine)", elevation = "Elevation (m)", tpi_300m = "Topographic position index (300 m)", slope = "Slope (degrees)", ruggedness = "Ruggedness", northness = "Northness", eastness = "Eastness") # groups of related predictors predictor_groups <- list(elevation_position = c("elevation", "tpi_300m"), steepness = c("slope", "ruggedness"), aspect = c("northness", "eastness"), time_of_day = "day_fraction", season = c("yday_sin", "yday_cos")) group_labels <- c(elevation_position = "Elevation & topographic position", steepness = "Slope & ruggedness", aspect = "Aspect (northness & eastness)", time_of_day = "Time of day (day fraction)", season = "Day of year (sine & cosine)") ``` ::: ## Missing values Unlike `ranger`, XGBoost can use rows with missing values - at each split, it learns which branch the missing values should go down. However, here the missing values are mostly over the sea (where the rasters are NA), which isn't 'unknown' terrain but a different surface altogether, and the random forest couldn't use these bouts. We therefore remove them, so that the two methods are fitted to exactly the same bouts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # why each bout has missing values (if it does) combined_bouts %>% mutate(missing = case_when(is.na(elevation) ~ "over the sea (no elevation)", if_any(all_of(predictors), is.na) ~ "on the coast (no slope, ruggedness or aspect)", TRUE ~ "no missing values")) %>% count(missing, behaviour) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = behaviour, values_from = n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # the data for the models - the bouts with all of the predictors, with the # behaviour as a factor (flapping first, so that soaring is the 'event') model_data <- combined_bouts %>% drop_na(all_of(predictors)) %>% mutate(behaviour = factor(behaviour, levels = c("flapping", "soaring"))) # use a random 20% of the days when testing changes to the script if (test_run) { set.seed(seed) test_days <- sample(unique(model_data$date_local), size = round(0.2 * n_distinct(model_data$date_local))) model_data <- model_data %>% filter(date_local %in% test_days) } # number of bouts of each behaviour used in the models model_data %>% count(behaviour) %>% mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Spatial layers The spatial layers are only used for the prediction maps at the end of the script. They are cropped to the area around all of the bouts (plus a buffer), in the same way as in the random forest script. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the spatial layers to crop raster_files <- c(elevation = "mapping/HS_DEM.tif", tpi_300m = "mapping/TPI_300m.tif", slope = "mapping/HS_Slope.tif", ruggedness = "mapping/HS_Ruggedness.tif", aspect = "mapping/Aspect_degrees.tif") # the area to crop to - the extent of all of the flight locations plus a buffer (m) buffer_m <- 2000 crop_area <- ext(min(combined_bouts$utme) - buffer_m, max(combined_bouts$utme) + buffer_m, min(combined_bouts$utmn) - buffer_m, max(combined_bouts$utmn) + buffer_m) %>% # the eagle locations are in GDA94 / MGA zone 55 vect(crs = "EPSG:28355") # read in and crop each raster (the crop area is projected to the crs of each # raster, in case some are in a different crs) spatial_layers <- map(raster_files, \(f) { r <- rast(f) crop(r, project(crop_area, crs(r))) }) ``` ::: # Validation design We use the same cross-validation schemes as for the random forest (see that script for why random splits are misleading for these data): - **Day-blocked cross-validation** - all of the bouts from the same date are in the same fold, which tests prediction to new days - **Spatial block cross-validation** - 2 km square blocks are assigned to folds, which tests prediction to new places [@Valavi2019-sz] - **Random 10-fold cross-validation** - only as a reference for how optimistic (or otherwise misleading) a random split is - **Leave-one-bird-out cross-validation** - only when there is more than one eagle in the data The folds are made with exactly the same code and seed as in the random forest script, so each bout is in the same fold for both methods. This means that the two methods are tested on exactly the same held-out data, and can be compared fold by fold. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(seed) # random folds - each bout is assigned to a fold at random model_data <- model_data %>% mutate(fold_random = sample(rep(1:n_folds_random, length.out = n()))) # day folds - each date is assigned to a fold at random, and every bout on that # date gets the same fold day_folds <- model_data %>% distinct(date_local) %>% mutate(fold_day = sample(rep(1:n_folds_day, length.out = n()))) model_data <- model_data %>% left_join(day_folds, by = "date_local") # bird folds - one fold for each eagle (only when there is more than one eagle) if (n_distinct(model_data$name) > 1) { model_data <- model_data %>% mutate(fold_bird = as.integer(factor(name))) } # spatial folds - square blocks assigned to folds at random (of 100 random # assignments, cv_spatial keeps the one with the most even folds) bouts_sf <- st_as_sf(model_data, coords = c("utme", "utmn"), crs = "EPSG:28355", remove = FALSE) spatial_cv <- cv_spatial(x = bouts_sf, column = "soaring", size = block_size_m, k = n_folds_spatial, hexagon = FALSE, selection = "random", iteration = 100, seed = seed, biomod2 = FALSE, progress = FALSE, report = FALSE, plot = FALSE) model_data$fold_spatial <- spatial_cv$folds_ids # the cross-validation schemes, and the column with the folds for each cv_schemes <- c(random = "fold_random", day = "fold_day", spatial = "fold_spatial") if ("fold_bird" %in% names(model_data)) cv_schemes <- c(cv_schemes, bird = "fold_bird") cv_scheme_labels <- c(random = "Random 10-fold (reference only)", day = "Day-blocked", spatial = "Spatial blocks", bird = "Leave-one-bird-out") # number of bouts and proportion of soaring bouts in each fold model_data %>% pivot_longer(all_of(unname(cv_schemes)), names_to = "scheme", values_to = "fold") %>% group_by(scheme, fold) %>% summarise(n_bouts = n(), prop_soaring = round(mean(soaring), 2), .groups = "drop") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = scheme, values_from = c(n_bouts, prop_soaring)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Check that the folds match the random forest If the random forest script has been run, we check that each bout is in the same fold as in the random forest's out-of-fold predictions. The number of bouts in a different fold should be 0. This check (and the comparison with the random forest below) is skipped when `test_run` is `TRUE`, as the folds are then made on the subset of days, so they won't match. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf_oof_file <- file.path(rf_dir, "rf_oof_predictions.csv") if (file.exists(rf_oof_file) && !test_run) { rf_folds <- read_csv(rf_oof_file, show_col_types = FALSE) %>% filter(model == "full") %>% select(bout_id, scheme, rf_fold = fold) model_data %>% select(bout_id, all_of(unname(cv_schemes))) %>% pivot_longer(-bout_id, names_to = "scheme", values_to = "fold") %>% mutate(scheme = str_remove(scheme, "fold_")) %>% inner_join(rf_folds, by = c("bout_id", "scheme")) %>% group_by(scheme) %>% summarise(n_bouts_compared = n(), n_in_a_different_fold = sum(fold != rf_fold)) } else { "The random forest outputs weren't found (or this is a test run), so the folds can't be compared" } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: # XGBoost models ## How XGBoost differs from a random forest Both methods combine many decision trees, but in different ways: - A **random forest** grows many deep trees independently, each on a random sample of the data, and averages them. Adding more trees doesn't over-fit - the average just becomes more stable. - **Gradient boosting** (XGBoost, @Chen2016-gk) grows shallow trees one after another. Each new tree is fitted to the errors of the model so far (the gradient of the log loss), and its predictions are shrunk by the learning rate before being added on. The model is built up on the log-odds scale, so the predicted probability of soaring is the logistic transform of the sum of the trees. Because each tree corrects the previous ones, adding too many trees *does* over-fit, so the number of boosting rounds has to be chosen with held-out data. The main XGBoost settings are: - `learning_rate` (eta) - how much each tree contributes. Smaller values need more rounds but usually give better predictions. We fix it at 0.05, and choose the number of rounds with early stopping. - `nrounds` - the number of boosting rounds (trees). We use **early stopping** - the model keeps adding trees until the log loss of the held-out folds hasn't improved for 50 rounds, and the best number of rounds is kept. - `max_depth` - the depth of each tree. This sets the highest order of interaction a single tree can fit (a depth of 2 allows two-way interactions, such as slope × time of day). - `min_child_weight` - the smallest 'weight' (for a binary response, the sum of p × (1 - p) of the bouts) in a terminal node. Larger values stop the trees fitting small groups of bouts. With probabilities near 0.5, a weight of 10 is roughly 40 bouts. - `subsample` - the proportion of the bouts used to grow each tree (like the random forest's sample fraction) - `colsample_bynode` - the proportion of the predictors that each split can choose from (like the random forest's `mtry`). We fix it at 0.8. We use the log loss (the negative log-likelihood of the observed behaviour under the predicted probabilities) for early stopping and to choose between settings, as this is what XGBoost minimises and it rewards well-calibrated probabilities. We also report the AUC. ## Helper functions As for the random forest, three small functions make sure that every model is fitted, predicted and evaluated in the same way. `cv_metrics()` is the same as in the random forest script. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the XGBoost parameters, from one row of the tuning grid xgb_settings <- function(p) { xgb.params(objective = "binary:logistic", # the last metric is used for early stopping eval_metric = c("auc", "logloss"), learning_rate = learning_rate, max_depth = p$max_depth, min_child_weight = p$min_child_weight, subsample = p$subsample, colsample_bynode = 0.8, nthread = n_threads, seed = seed) } # fit an XGBoost model of soaring (1) vs flapping (0), using the variables in vars fit_xgb <- function(data, vars, params, nrounds) { train_matrix <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(data[vars]), label = data$soaring, nthread = n_threads) xgb.train(params = xgb_settings(params), data = train_matrix, nrounds = nrounds, verbose = 0) } # predicted probability of soaring (XGBoost needs exactly the columns it was # trained with, in the same order, so we select them by name) predict_soaring <- function(model, newdata) { predict(model, as.matrix(newdata[variable.names(model)])) } # AUC, TSS (with the sensitivity, specificity and threshold) and Brier score cv_metrics <- function(observed, predicted) { roc_curve <- pROC::roc(response = observed, predictor = predicted, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE) # the threshold that maximises sensitivity + specificity - 1 (i.e. TSS) best <- pROC::coords(roc_curve, x = "best", best.method = "youden", ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"), transpose = FALSE)[1, ] tibble(AUC = as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_curve)), TSS = best$sensitivity + best$specificity - 1, sensitivity = best$sensitivity, specificity = best$specificity, threshold = best$threshold, Brier = mean((predicted - observed)^2)) } ``` ::: ## Tuning the tree settings and the number of rounds For every combination of settings in `tuning_grid`, we run `xgb.cv` with the day-blocked folds. For each combination, early stopping finds the number of rounds with the lowest held-out log loss, and we keep the combination with the lowest log loss overall. As for the random forest, the tuning isn't repeated inside each fold of each cross-validation scheme (nested cross-validation), so the cross-validated metrics below are slightly optimistic. Here this also applies to the number of rounds, which is chosen with the same day folds that are used to test the models. The spatial cross-validation uses the same settings, so it isn't affected in the same way. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tuning_grid <- expand_grid(max_depth = c(2, 3, 4, 6), min_child_weight = c(1, 10, 50), subsample = c(0.5, 0.8)) # the held-out bouts (row numbers) of each day fold, for xgb.cv day_fold_rows <- map(sort(unique(model_data$fold_day)), \(k) which(model_data$fold_day == k)) # all of the bouts as an XGBoost data matrix all_bouts_matrix <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(model_data[predictors]), label = model_data$soaring, nthread = n_threads) start_time <- Sys.time() tuning_results <- list() tuning_logs <- list() for (i in 1:nrow(tuning_grid)) { cv <- xgb.cv(params = xgb_settings(tuning_grid[i, ]), data = all_bouts_matrix, nrounds = max_rounds, folds = day_fold_rows, early_stopping_rounds = early_stopping_rounds, verbose = 0) # the held-out metrics at the best number of rounds best_round <- cv$early_stop$best_iteration best_log <- cv$evaluation_log[best_round, ] tuning_results[[i]] <- bind_cols(tuning_grid[i, ], nrounds = best_round, test_logloss = best_log$test_logloss_mean, test_auc = best_log$test_auc_mean, train_auc = best_log$train_auc_mean) # the metrics at every round (for the learning curves) tuning_logs[[i]] <- as_tibble(cv$evaluation_log) %>% mutate(setting = i) } tuning_results <- bind_rows(tuning_results) %>% mutate(setting = row_number()) %>% arrange(test_logloss) # time taken to tune Sys.time() - start_time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time difference of 55.92466 secs ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} tuning_results %>% mutate(across(c(test_logloss, test_auc, train_auc), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # the best settings best_params <- tuning_results %>% slice(1) %>% select(max_depth, min_child_weight, subsample) best_params ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Learning curves The training and held-out (day-blocked) log loss and AUC at each boosting round, for the best settings. The shaded bands are ± 1 standard deviation across the folds, and the dashed line is the number of rounds chosen by early stopping. The training performance keeps improving as more trees are added, but the held-out performance levels off and then gets worse - the gap between them is the over-fitting. Early stopping picks the number of rounds where the held-out log loss is lowest. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best_setting <- tuning_results$setting[1] tuning_logs[[best_setting]] %>% pivot_longer(-c(iter, setting), names_to = c("data", "metric", ".value"), names_pattern = "(train|test)_(auc|logloss)_(mean|std)") %>% mutate(data = if_else(data == "train", "Training folds", "Held-out folds (day-blocked)"), metric = if_else(metric == "auc", "AUC", "Log loss")) %>% ggplot(aes(x = iter, y = mean, colour = data, fill = data)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - std, ymax = mean + std), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) + geom_line() + geom_vline(xintercept = tuning_results$nrounds[1], linetype = "dashed") + facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00")) + labs(x = "Boosting round (number of trees)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png) ::: ::: ## Number of rounds for each model As for the random forest, we compare four models: **null** (the proportion of soaring bouts in the training data), **time** (only the time of day and day of year), **landscape** (only the topographic variables) and **full** (both). Unlike the random forest, the best number of rounds depends a lot on how much signal there is in the predictors, so we use early stopping (with the day folds and the best tree settings) to choose the number of rounds separately for each model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the variables in each model model_sets <- list(time = time_vars, landscape = landscape_vars, full = predictors) model_nrounds <- map_dbl(model_sets, \(vars) { model_matrix <- xgb.DMatrix(as.matrix(model_data[vars]), label = model_data$soaring, nthread = n_threads) cv <- xgb.cv(params = xgb_settings(best_params), data = model_matrix, nrounds = max_rounds, folds = day_fold_rows, early_stopping_rounds = early_stopping_rounds, verbose = 0) cv$early_stop$best_iteration }) model_nrounds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` time landscape full 3 28 40 ``` ::: ::: ## Cross-validation of the four models Each model is fitted to the training folds and predicts the held-out fold, for each cross-validation scheme. We keep the full model fitted in each day and spatial fold, for the permutation importance and the uncertainty in the prediction maps. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} start_time <- Sys.time() oof_predictions <- list() fold_models <- list() for (scheme in names(cv_schemes)) { fold_col <- cv_schemes[[scheme]] fold_models[[scheme]] <- list() for (k in sort(unique(model_data[[fold_col]]))) { train <- model_data %>% filter(.data[[fold_col]] != k) test <- model_data %>% filter(.data[[fold_col]] == k) # the null model predicts the proportion of soaring bouts in the training data predictions <- tibble(bout_id = test$bout_id, scheme = scheme, fold = k, soaring = test$soaring, null = mean(train$soaring)) # fit and predict each of the XGBoost models for (m in names(model_sets)) { fit <- fit_xgb(train, model_sets[[m]], best_params, model_nrounds[[m]]) predictions[[m]] <- predict_soaring(fit, test) # keep the full models (not for the random folds, which aren't used below) if (m == "full" && scheme != "random") fold_models[[scheme]][[as.character(k)]] <- fit } oof_predictions[[paste(scheme, k)]] <- predictions } } # one row for each bout, scheme and model oof_predictions <- bind_rows(oof_predictions) %>% pivot_longer(c(null, time, landscape, full), names_to = "model", values_to = "prob") %>% mutate(model = factor(model, levels = c("null", "time", "landscape", "full"))) # time taken for the cross-validation Sys.time() - start_time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time difference of 1.937898 secs ``` ::: ::: ## Results The metrics are calculated from the out-of-fold predictions of all of the bouts pooled together, along with the mean and standard deviation of the AUC across the folds. The day-blocked and spatial block results are the ones to use. As for the random forest, the AUC can be below 0.5. For the null model this is an artefact of pooling the folds (its AUC within each fold is exactly 0.5). This is the model used for the SHAP values, effect plots and prediction maps below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final_model <- fit_xgb(model_data, predictors, best_params, model_nrounds[["full"]]) final_model ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ##### xgb.Booster call: xgb.train(params = xgb_settings(params), data = train_matrix, nrounds = nrounds, verbose = 0) # of features: 9 # of rounds: 40 ``` ::: ::: # Interpretation ## XGBoost's built-in importance XGBoost reports three measures of importance for each variable, all calculated from the trees of the final model (i.e. the training data): - **Gain** - the total improvement in the log loss from the splits on that variable (the most commonly used) - **Cover** - the number of bouts (weighted) affected by the splits on that variable - **Frequency** - the proportion of all splits that are on that variable These are shown for reference only. They measure how much the model *used* each variable to fit the training data, not how much each variable helps to predict new data, and they share out the credit between correlated variables (such as slope and ruggedness) fairly arbitrarily. Gain also favours continuous variables with many possible split points. We therefore use the permutation importance and the SHAP values below as the main results. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xgb.importance(model = final_model) %>% as_tibble() %>% pivot_longer(c(Gain, Cover, Frequency), names_to = "measure", values_to = "importance") %>% mutate(label = variable_labels[Feature], measure = factor(measure, levels = c("Gain", "Cover", "Frequency"))) %>% ggplot(aes(x = importance, y = reorder(label, importance))) + geom_col(fill = "grey50") + facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = "Proportion of the total", y = NULL) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png) ::: ::: ## Permutation importance The same as for the random forest - for each full model from the day-blocked and spatial cross-validation folds, we shuffle one variable (or group of variables) in the held-out bouts, and measure how much the AUC drops. Shuffling a group of variables together is preferred when the variables are correlated (see the random forest script for why). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # each variable on its own, and each group of variables importance_sets <- c(set_names(as.list(predictors)), predictor_groups) importance_types <- c(rep("Single variable", length(predictors)), rep("Group of variables", length(predictor_groups))) names(importance_types) <- names(importance_sets) # AUC from the observed behaviour and predicted probability auc_value <- function(observed, predicted) { as.numeric(pROC::auc(observed, predicted, levels = c(0, 1), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)) } set.seed(seed) start_time <- Sys.time() importance_results <- list() for (scheme in names(fold_models)) { fold_col <- cv_schemes[[scheme]] for (k in names(fold_models[[scheme]])) { fit <- fold_models[[scheme]][[k]] test <- model_data %>% filter(.data[[fold_col]] == as.numeric(k)) # AUC of the held-out bouts before shuffling auc_original <- auc_value(test$soaring, predict_soaring(fit, test)) for (set_name in names(importance_sets)) { vars <- importance_sets[[set_name]] for (i in 1:n_permutations) { # shuffle the rows of these variables (in the same order for every # variable in a group, so their combinations stay the same) shuffled <- test new_order <- sample(nrow(test)) shuffled[vars] <- test[new_order, vars] importance_results[[length(importance_results) + 1]] <- tibble(scheme = scheme, fold = k, set = set_name, type = importance_types[[set_name]], permutation = i, auc_drop = auc_original - auc_value(test$soaring, predict_soaring(fit, shuffled))) } } } } importance_results <- bind_rows(importance_results) # time taken for the permutation importance Sys.time() - start_time ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Time difference of 2.777027 secs ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # average over the permutations in each fold, then the mean and SD across folds importance_summary <- importance_results %>% group_by(scheme, type, set, fold) %>% summarise(auc_drop = mean(auc_drop), .groups = "drop") %>% group_by(scheme, type, set) %>% summarise(mean_auc_drop = mean(auc_drop), sd_auc_drop = sd(auc_drop), .groups = "drop") ``` ::: The drop in AUC when each group (left) or variable (right) is shuffled. The error bars are ± 1 standard deviation across the folds. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} importance_summary %>% mutate(label = c(group_labels, variable_labels)[set], type = factor(type, levels = c("Group of variables", "Single variable")), scheme = cv_scheme_labels[scheme]) %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean_auc_drop, y = reorder(label, mean_auc_drop), fill = scheme)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = mean_auc_drop - sd_auc_drop, xmax = mean_auc_drop + sd_auc_drop), position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.3) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) + facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") + scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey40", "grey75")) + labs(x = "Drop in AUC when shuffled", y = NULL, fill = "Cross-validation") + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png) ::: ::: ## SHAP values SHAP values split each bout's prediction into a contribution from each variable (Lundberg & Lee 2017, *A unified approach to interpreting model predictions*). For each bout, the prediction (on the log-odds scale) is the average prediction plus the sum of the SHAP values of all of the variables, so a SHAP value of 0.2 for slope means that the slope at that bout's location raised its log-odds of soaring by 0.2 compared to the average. XGBoost calculates them exactly for tree models (TreeSHAP), so they are quick to calculate for every bout. Unlike the permutation importance (one number per variable) and ALE (the average effect), SHAP values show the effect of each variable for every bout, so we can see whether the effect of a variable depends on the values of other variables (e.g. the time of day). Two caveats. SHAP values are calculated with the final model on the training data, so (like XGBoost's built-in importance) they describe how the model uses each variable, not how well it predicts new data. And with correlated predictors, the credit can still be shared between them, so we also sum the SHAP values of each group of predictors (SHAP values add up, so the SHAP value of a group is the sum of the SHAP values of its variables). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # SHAP values of every bout (one column per variable, plus the intercept, which # is the same for every bout) bout_matrix <- as.matrix(model_data[predictors]) shap_matrix <- predict(final_model, bout_matrix, predcontrib = TRUE) # check - the intercept plus the SHAP values of each bout should equal the # model's prediction on the log-odds scale (the largest difference should be ~0) max(abs(rowSums(shap_matrix) - predict(final_model, bout_matrix, outputmargin = TRUE))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.146699e-07 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # one row for each bout and variable, with the value of the variable and its SHAP value shap_long <- as_tibble(shap_matrix[, predictors]) %>% mutate(row = row_number()) %>% pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "variable", values_to = "shap") %>% left_join(model_data %>% select(all_of(predictors)) %>% mutate(row = row_number()) %>% pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value"), by = c("row", "variable")) ``` ::: ### SHAP importance The mean absolute SHAP value of each variable and each group of variables - the average size of its effect on the log-odds of soaring. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shap_importance <- bind_rows( # each variable on its own shap_long %>% group_by(set = variable) %>% summarise(mean_abs_shap = mean(abs(shap))) %>% mutate(type = "Single variable"), # each group of variables (the sum of the SHAP values of the variables in the group) imap(predictor_groups, \(vars, g) { tibble(set = g, mean_abs_shap = mean(abs(rowSums(shap_matrix[, vars, drop = FALSE])))) }) %>% bind_rows() %>% mutate(type = "Group of variables") ) shap_importance %>% mutate(label = c(group_labels, variable_labels)[set], type = factor(type, levels = c("Group of variables", "Single variable"))) %>% ggplot(aes(x = mean_abs_shap, y = reorder(label, mean_abs_shap))) + geom_col(fill = "grey50") + facet_wrap(~ type, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "Mean absolute SHAP value (log-odds of soaring)", y = NULL) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png) ::: ::: ### SHAP summary plot Each point is one bout, placed by its SHAP value for that variable, and coloured by the value of the variable (from the lowest to the highest value in the data). The variables are ordered by their mean absolute SHAP value. For example, if the high values (yellow) are on the right, higher values of that variable increase the probability of soaring. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the order of the variables (most important at the top) variable_order <- shap_importance %>% filter(type == "Single variable") %>% arrange(mean_abs_shap) %>% pull(set) set.seed(seed) shap_long %>% # the value of each variable as a percentile (0 = lowest, 1 = highest) group_by(variable) %>% mutate(value_rank = percent_rank(value)) %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = variable_order, labels = variable_labels[variable_order])) %>% ggplot(aes(x = shap, y = variable, colour = value_rank)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.3, size = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) + scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma", breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("Low", "High")) + labs(x = "SHAP value (effect on the log-odds of soaring)", y = NULL, colour = "Value of\nthe variable") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png) ::: ::: ### Effects of the time variables The SHAP values of the day fraction, and of the day of year (the sum of the SHAP values of its sine and cosine, plotted against the day of year). Each point is a bout and the line is a smooth through them. The spread of the points at the same value shows how much the effect depends on the other variables. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tibble( `Day fraction (0 = sunrise, 1 = sunset)` = model_data$day_fraction, `Day of the year` = model_data$yday, shap_day_fraction = shap_matrix[, "day_fraction"], shap_season = shap_matrix[, "yday_sin"] + shap_matrix[, "yday_cos"] ) %>% pivot_longer(c(`Day fraction (0 = sunrise, 1 = sunset)`, `Day of the year`), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>% mutate(shap = if_else(variable == "Day of the year", shap_season, shap_day_fraction)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = shap)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.1) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, colour = behaviour_colours[["soaring"]]) + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = "SHAP value (effect on the log-odds of soaring)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png) ::: ::: ### Do the landscape effects change with time? SHAP dependence plots for the three landscape variables with the largest mean absolute SHAP values. If the effect of the landscape changes with the time (an interaction), the colours will separate vertically - e.g. if steep slopes only raised the probability of soaring in the afternoon, the afternoon bouts would be higher than the morning bouts at steep slopes. ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Coloured by the time of day ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # plot in a random order, so no time of day is always on top slice_sample(prop = 1) %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = shap, colour = day_fraction)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") + scale_colour_viridis_c(option = "plasma") + labs(x = NULL, y = "SHAP value (log-odds of soaring)", colour = "Day\nfraction") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png) ::: ::: #### Coloured by the time of year ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dependence_data %>% slice_sample(prop = 1) %>% ggplot(aes(x = value, y = shap, colour = yday_cos)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") + scale_colour_distiller(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, limits = c(-1, 1), breaks = c(-1, 0, 1), labels = c("Mid-winter", "Autumn/spring", "Mid-summer")) + labs(x = NULL, y = "SHAP value (log-odds of soaring)", colour = "Time of year") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png) ::: ::: ::: ### SHAP interaction values XGBoost can also split each SHAP value into a main effect and the interactions with each of the other variables (SHAP interaction values). The heat map shows the mean absolute interaction value for each pair of variables (the main effects, on the diagonal, are left out). A larger value means the model's prediction depends more on that *combination* of variables, beyond their separate effects. The interactions between the time variables and the landscape variables are the ones that show whether the eagles use the landscape differently at different times. The interaction values take longer to calculate, so we use a random sample of up to 2500 soaring and 2500 flapping bouts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # a random sample of bouts, with the same number of each behaviour set.seed(seed) interaction_sample <- model_data %>% group_by(behaviour) %>% slice_sample(n = 2500) %>% ungroup() # SHAP interaction values - an array with one row for each bout, and one # column and layer for each variable (plus the intercept) shap_interactions <- predict(final_model, as.matrix(interaction_sample[predictors]), predinteraction = TRUE) # mean absolute interaction value for each pair of variables interaction_strength <- apply(abs(shap_interactions[, predictors, predictors]), c(2, 3), mean) interaction_table <- interaction_strength %>% as_tibble(rownames = "variable_1") %>% pivot_longer(-variable_1, names_to = "variable_2", values_to = "interaction") %>% mutate(type = case_when(variable_1 == variable_2 ~ "main effect", variable_1 %in% time_vars & variable_2 %in% time_vars ~ "time x time", variable_1 %in% landscape_vars & variable_2 %in% landscape_vars ~ "landscape x landscape", TRUE ~ "time x landscape")) interaction_table %>% # leave out the main effects mutate(interaction = if_else(type == "main effect", NA, interaction), across(c(variable_1, variable_2), \(x) factor(x, levels = predictors))) %>% ggplot(aes(x = variable_1, y = variable_2, fill = interaction)) + geom_tile() + # label the interactions (not the empty main effect cells) geom_text(data = \(d) filter(d, !is.na(interaction)), aes(label = round(interaction, 3)), size = 2.8) + scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Mean absolute\ninteraction\nvalue") + theme_bw() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png) ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # the total size of the main effects and of each type of interaction. Each pair # appears twice in the matrix (the interaction is split equally between them) interaction_table %>% group_by(type) %>% summarise(total = sum(interaction)) %>% mutate(proportion = round(total / sum(total), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Accumulated local effects The same accumulated local effects (ALE) plots as for the random forest [@Apley2020-iu], which show how the predicted probability of soaring changes with each variable (on the probability scale, centred so that the average effect is 0). These are directly comparable to the random forest's ALE plots. The rug at the bottom of each panel shows the values in the data (a random sample of 1000 bouts). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # iml needs the model, the predictor data and a function that returns the # predicted probability of soaring xgb_predictor <- Predictor$new(model = final_model, data = model_data %>% select(all_of(predictors)) %>% as.data.frame(), predict.function = \(model, newdata) predict_soaring(model, newdata)) ale_vars <- c("day_fraction", landscape_vars) ale_results <- map(ale_vars, \(v) { FeatureEffect$new(xgb_predictor, feature = v, method = "ale", grid.size = 40)$results %>% rename(value = all_of(v), ale = .value) %>% mutate(variable = v) }) %>% bind_rows() # a sample of the data for the rug set.seed(seed) rug_data <- model_data %>% slice_sample(n = min(1000, nrow(model_data))) %>% select(all_of(ale_vars)) %>% pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable") bind_rows(ale = ale_results, rug = rug_data, .id = "data") %>% mutate(variable = factor(variable_labels[variable], levels = variable_labels)) %>% ggplot(aes(x = value)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_line(data = \(d) filter(d, data == "ale"), aes(y = ale), colour = behaviour_colours[["soaring"]], linewidth = 1) + geom_rug(data = \(d) filter(d, data == "rug"), alpha = 0.2, length = unit(0.03, "npc")) + facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Effect on the probability of soaring (ALE)") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png) ::: ::: ## Time of day through the year The average predicted probability of soaring for each day fraction and day of the year, from moving a random sample of bouts to each combination (averaged over the landscape variables of the sampled bouts), the same as for the random forest. The day fractions are limited to the range in the data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # a random sample of bouts to average over set.seed(seed) bout_sample <- model_data %>% slice_sample(n = min(400, nrow(model_data))) # every combination of day fraction (every 0.025, within the range of the data) # and day of year (every week) time_grid <- expand_grid(day_fraction = seq(floor(min(model_data$day_fraction) * 40) / 40, ceiling(max(model_data$day_fraction) * 40) / 40, by = 0.025), yday = seq(1, 365, by = 7)) # every sampled bout at every combination of day fraction and day of year time_effect <- bout_sample %>% select(bout_id, all_of(landscape_vars)) %>% cross_join(time_grid) %>% mutate(yday_sin = sin(2 * pi * yday / 365.25), yday_cos = cos(2 * pi * yday / 365.25)) time_effect$prob <- predict_soaring(final_model, time_effect) time_effect %>% group_by(day_fraction, yday) %>% summarise(prob = mean(prob), .groups = "drop") %>% ggplot() + geom_raster(aes(x = yday, y = day_fraction, fill = prob)) + # solar noon is (very close to) halfway between sunrise and sunset geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = "white", linetype = "dashed") + scale_fill_viridis_c() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = yday(make_date(2021, 1:12, 1)), labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1), expand = c(0, 0)) + labs(x = "Day of the year", y = "Day fraction (0 = sunrise, 1 = sunset)", fill = "Probability\nof soaring") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png) ::: ::: # Prediction maps The same maps as for the random forest - the final model is predicted to every 30 m cell in the study area, in the middle of summer (15 January) and winter (15 July), at day fractions of 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. **These maps show the relative suitability for soaring, not the probability that an eagle soars there** - a high value means that if the eagle is flying there at that time, it is more likely to be soaring than flapping. Cells where any landscape variable is outside the range of the bouts used to fit the model are masked (grey). ## Prediction data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # project each layer to the elevation grid (nearest neighbour keeps the values the same) prediction_stack <- map(names(spatial_layers), \(layer) { r <- spatial_layers[[layer]] if (layer != "elevation") r <- project(r, spatial_layers$elevation, method = "near") names(r) <- layer r }) %>% rast() # northness and eastness from aspect (flat cells, with an aspect of -1, are 0) prediction_stack$northness <- ifel(prediction_stack$aspect == -1, 0, cos(prediction_stack$aspect * pi / 180)) prediction_stack$eastness <- ifel(prediction_stack$aspect == -1, 0, sin(prediction_stack$aspect * pi / 180)) # one row for each cell with all of the landscape variables (i.e. on land). # (when these are plotted with geom_raster, ggplot warns that the pixels are at # 'uneven intervals' - this is because some rows of cells are all sea, and can be # ignored, as the cells are still on a regular 30 m grid) grid_df <- as.data.frame(prediction_stack[[landscape_vars]], xy = TRUE, cells = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) # cells where every landscape variable is within the range of the model data grid_df$in_range <- TRUE for (v in landscape_vars) { grid_df$in_range <- grid_df$in_range & grid_df[[v]] >= min(model_data[[v]]) & grid_df[[v]] <= max(model_data[[v]]) } # the days of the year and day fractions to predict for scenario_ydays <- c(15, 196) scenario_day_fractions <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75) # sunrise and sunset (local time) on each scenario day at the centre of the # study area - only used to show the clock times of each scenario scenario_sun_times <- getSunlightTimes(date = make_date(2021, 1, 1) + scenario_ydays - 1, lat = mean(model_data$lat), lon = mean(model_data$lon), keep = c("sunrise", "sunset"), tz = local_tz) %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(yday = yday(date)) %>% select(yday, sunrise, sunset) scenarios <- expand_grid(yday = scenario_ydays, day_fraction = scenario_day_fractions) %>% left_join(scenario_sun_times, by = "yday") %>% mutate(season = if_else(yday == 15, "Summer (15 January)", "Winter (15 July)"), time = factor(paste("Day fraction", day_fraction), levels = paste("Day fraction", scenario_day_fractions)), # the local clock time of this day fraction clock_time = format(sunrise + day_fraction * (sunset - sunrise), "%H:%M"), # a short name for each scenario (for the raster layers) name = paste0("yday", yday, "_dayfrac", day_fraction)) scenarios %>% select(season, time, clock_time) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Predict ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scenario_predictions <- map(1:nrow(scenarios), \(i) { # the landscape of every cell, with the time variables of this scenario newdata <- grid_df %>% mutate(day_fraction = scenarios$day_fraction[i], yday_sin = sin(2 * pi * scenarios$yday[i] / 365.25), yday_cos = cos(2 * pi * scenarios$yday[i] / 365.25)) grid_df %>% select(cell, x, y, in_range) %>% mutate(prob = predict_soaring(final_model, newdata), name = scenarios$name[i], season = scenarios$season[i], time = scenarios$time[i]) }) %>% bind_rows() scenario_predictions %>% # mask the cells outside the range of the data mutate(prob = if_else(in_range, prob, NA)) %>% ggplot() + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = prob)) + facet_grid(season ~ time) + # the colour scale covers the range of the predictions (the same for every map) scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey70") + coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Relative\nsoaring\nsuitability") + theme_bw() + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png) ::: ::: ## Uncertainty The standard deviation of the predictions from the five full models fitted in the spatial cross-validation folds, halfway through the day (day fraction 0.5) in summer and winter. predictions of each spatial fold model (one column per model) fold_predictions <- map(fold_models$spatial, \(fit) predict_soaring(fit, newdata)) %>% bind_cols() grid_df %>% select(cell, x, y, in_range) %>% mutate(sd = apply(fold_predictions, 1, sd), name = paste0(noon_scenarios$name[i], "_sd"), season = noon_scenarios$season[i]) }) %>% bind_rows() uncertainty %>% mutate(sd = if_else(in_range, sd, NA)) %>% ggplot() + geom_raster(aes(x = x, y = y, fill = sd)) + facet_wrap(~ season) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", na.value = "grey70") + coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "SD across\nspatial fold\nmodels") + theme_bw() + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](energy_harvesting_XGBoost_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png) ::: ::: # Summary of the results ::: {.callout-note} These notes describe the results for Tabatha when this script was written (November 2026). The numbers are filled in when the script is run, but the interpretation will need checking if the data change (e.g. when more eagles are added). ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # AUC of a model (from the pooled out-of-fold predictions) for the text below auc_of <- function(results, s, m) { if (is.null(results)) return(NA) round(results$AUC[results$scheme == s & results$model == m], 3) } # the random forest results (if they exist) rf_cv_results <- if (file.exists(rf_results_file)) read_csv(rf_results_file, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL # the share of the SHAP interaction values from each type of effect (%) interaction_share <- interaction_table %>% group_by(type) %>% summarise(total = sum(interaction)) %>% mutate(percent = round(100 * total / sum(total))) share_of <- function(t) interaction_share$percent[interaction_share$type == t] ``` ::: - **XGBoost performs about the same as the random forest.** The full model has an AUC of 0.542 for new days (random forest 0.547) and 0.503 for new areas (random forest 0.506), so neither method predicts new areas much better than chance. The fold-by-fold comparison shows that the two methods have similar AUCs for most folds. This suggests that the limit is the information in the predictors, rather than the method. - **The tuning made little difference.** Many combinations of settings had almost the same held-out log loss. Early stopping chose 40 rounds for the full model (with a maximum tree depth of 6), and the learning curves show that the training performance keeps improving after this while the held-out performance levels off at an AUC of about 0.55. - **As for the random forest, what skill there is comes from the landscape.** The landscape-only model is as good as the full model (AUC 0.55 for new days), and the time-only model is close to chance (0.501). The most important groups of variables (permutation importance) for new days are elevation & topographic position, slope & ruggedness, and aspect, while for new areas aspect and slope & ruggedness are more important than elevation & topographic position. The variables with the largest SHAP values are elevation, the topographic position index and eastness. - **The directions of the effects match the random forest.** Soaring is more likely at locations that are lower than their surroundings (negative TPI) and at elevations of about 680 to 750 m, and less likely at locations that are higher than their surroundings (positive TPI), at elevations above about 750 m and over east-facing slopes. - **The time variables have small effects.** Soaring is relatively less likely just after sunrise and in the last quarter of the day, and less likely in autumn (around March and April) than in late winter and late spring, but these shifts are too small for the time-only model to separate soaring from flapping. - **There is little evidence that the landscape effects change with the time.** The interactions between the time and landscape variables make up 24% of the SHAP interaction values (the main effects make up 37%, and the interactions among the landscape variables 37%), and the SHAP dependence plots mostly don't separate by the time of day or year (apart from a hint that west-facing slopes are used for soaring more in winter than in summer). This agrees with the random forest's ALE curves for subsets of the bouts. The suggestions for improving the models at the end of the random forest script (multi-scale and path-averaged landscape variables, wind, land cover, and more eagles) apply equally here. # References ::: {#refs} ::: # Session Information ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} utils::sessionInfo() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R version 4.5.0 (2025-04-11) Platform: aarch64-apple-darwin20 Running under: macOS 26.6.2 Matrix products: default BLAS: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.5-arm64/Resources/lib/libRblas.0.dylib LAPACK: /Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Versions/4.5-arm64/Resources/lib/libRlapack.dylib;
